Foundation examination: Volumes1–4

Volume 04 · Chapter 12

Empirical integration and replication

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v04-c11

By the endReproduce a small empirical result and document departures from the original analysis.

Make an empirical claim reproducible at its actual scope

Capability: reconstruct a small published empirical result from a documented historical source, explain numerical departures, and write a replication report that separates what was reproduced from what remains unverified. Prerequisite: computational reliability and numerical audits. Earlier chapters supply data contracts, descriptive analysis, causal identification and timing-aware prediction.

A report says that the United States unemployment rate rose to 4.3% in July 2024. Repeating that sentence is citation. Recovering its numerator and denominator from the appropriate archived table, calculating the rate, matching the published precision and preserving every input is a small empirical reconstruction. Rebuilding the survey weights and seasonal adjustment from person-level records would be a much larger replication. Success at the first task does not establish success at the second.

This chapter performs the first task with actual historical survey estimates. The six source records below are not synthetic observations. All teaching calculations, exercises and code are original. The narrow empirical target is useful because its departures reveal the consequences of units, vintages, rounding, definitions and research discretion without hiding those choices inside a large statistical package.

Freeze a claim before calculating

A replicable claim has a target, a source version, a transformation and a comparison rule. Our baseline is the household-survey TOTAL unemployment statistic in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Employment Situation — July 2024, release USDL-24-1571, published 2 August 2024 at 08:30 Eastern Daylight Time. Use its Table A-1, seasonally adjusted (SA) columns, July and June 2024. Reconstruct July's rate, its monthly change, and the change in the unemployed level. The published targets are 4.3%, +0.2 percentage point and +352 thousand persons.

The targets come from the archived BLS release, its Household Survey Data narrative and complete Table A-1 header and TOTAL rows. Observation month, publication time and retrieval date are different: July 2024 describes the observation period; 2 August 2024 identifies the release vintage; 7 October 2026 records our source inspection. Nothing here is an observation of October 2026 unemployment.

The baseline transformation is 100 times unemployed persons divided by the civilian labor force. Our comparison rule is agreement at the source's one decimal place for the rate and monthly rate change, together with an exact integer-thousand comparison for the level change. Retain the unrounded rational result. A rate discrepancy of 0.047 percentage point is acceptable only if explained by the declared display rule; it is not a universal tolerance for every calculation.

We also declare a four-cell comparison grid: SA and not seasonally adjusted (NSA), each with July 2024 compared to June 2024 and to July 2023. Report every cell. Compare subtracting source-displayed rates with subtracting reconstructed ratios and rounding afterward. These are fixed teaching specifications chosen with the historical answer known, not a claim of prior research registration. In a new investigation, date and preserve the protocol before inspecting the relevant outcomes; mark later additions as exploratory and retain their results.

Recover the data and the meaning of each number

The Current Population Survey household statistics concern the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and over in the 50 states and District of Columbia. The labor force contains employed and unemployed persons. The unemployed generally have no job, are available for work and have actively searched during the preceding four weeks; people on temporary layoff expecting recall have a search exception. Receiving unemployment insurance is not the classification rule. BLS's CPS definitions explain these concepts. The archived release's technical note gives the corresponding definitions and the reference week, generally the calendar week containing the 12th.

Let P, L, E, U and N denote the published population, labor force, employed, unemployed and not-in-labor-force levels, respectively, all measured in thousands of persons. The unemployment rate is r = 100U/L percent. The participation rate, 100L/P, answers a different question. These levels are survey estimates of people, not the number of survey respondents and not establishment-survey payroll jobs.

Frozen Table A-1 TOTAL extract, 2 August 2024 vintage; all levels in thousands of persons

The full source has nine time/adjustment columns: three NSA columns followed by six SA columns. Our extract uses original positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and 9. Reading a row without its full header could silently mix columns. Table A-1 footnote 1 says the population itself is not seasonally adjusted; the same population estimates appear on both sides. The table also notes annual January population-control updates. The release's technical note describes seasonal adjustment and revisions. A current database may contain later revised values: that is another vintage, not a replacement for this baseline.

A small but auditable retrieval chain

The archived HTML was retrieved without an account or payment through the available web retrieval service. A separate direct download attempt returned HTTP 403. The local source extract is therefore explicitly a manual transcription from the successfully retrieved complete table, not a raw HTML download. It records the original URL, full column order, row labels, units, release time, selected values and access limitation. No unavailable webpage bytes are claimed to have been preserved.

The analysis JSON is a structured copy of that extract. The manifest records SHA-256 hashes for both local files. Comparing those copies catches a transformation error; comparing the printed values back to the official table addresses transcription. Agreement between two copies produced by one transcription is not independent empirical corroboration. A hash detects changed bytes relative to a trusted manifest, but does not prove that the bytes came from BLS. Someone can change a file and its manifest together; provenance still needs documented source inspection.

The BLS public-use statement places its publications in the public domain except previously copyrighted photographs and illustrations and requests attribution. This package includes only a small attributed numeric extract, with no emblem or images. Retrieval access and permission to reuse are separate fields in the record; a failed automated download does not make fabricated replacement data acceptable.

Worked example 1: reconstruct the monthly published result

Use July SA unemployment U = 7,163 and labor force L = 168,429, both in thousands. Because their units cancel, multiplying numerator and denominator by 1,000 would leave the ratio unchanged:

rJuly = 100(7,163/168,429) = 716,300/168,429 ≈ 4.252830570% → 4.3%.

June's corresponding ratio is 100(6,811/168,009) ≈ 4.053949491% → 4.1%. Subtraction before display gives 4.252830570 − 4.053949491 = 0.198881079 percentage point, which rounds to +0.2. Subtracting the two published one-decimal rates also gives 4.3 − 4.1 = 0.2 percentage point. Both operations agree for this pair, but they need not always agree.

The unemployed level change is 7,163 − 6,811 = 352 thousand persons, or 352,000 persons. July's level is 7.163 million, which rounds to the narrative's 7.2 million. All three primary targets match at their specified precision. The published 4.3 exceeds our unrounded ratio by about 0.047169430 percentage point. That is a display difference, not an estimated standard error.

The calculation does not reveal the exact rate computed from undisplayed full-precision estimates. It establishes that the supplied published aggregates reproduce the published display. Nor does it reconstruct survey weighting or seasonal-adjustment estimation. Those steps generated our inputs. Our result is conditional on their release-vintage values and definitions.

Explain discrepancies before changing code or inputs

A useful discrepancy log states the expected output, observed output, size and unit of the departure, proposed explanation, evidence and unresolved work. Keep the original record. A genuine data error should be corrected in a new version with a change note, never silently repaired to force agreement. Three classes matter here: a harmless display difference, a different statistical target, and a calculation or transcription failure. A match at one headline number cannot distinguish them alone.

Worked example 2: a disagreement caused by rounding order

July 2023 SA gives r2023 = 100(5,904/167,113) ≈ 3.532938790%, which rounds to 3.5%. The year comparison produces two legitimate descriptions:

Difference of displayed rates: 4.3 − 3.5 = 0.8 percentage point.
Difference of reconstructed ratios: 4.252830570 − 3.532938790 ≈ 0.719891780 percentage point → 0.7.

Rounding is nonlinear: R(a) − R(b) need not equal R(a − b). Here the July 2024 display error is about +0.047169430, while the July 2023 display error is about −0.032938790. Their difference, about +0.080108220 percentage point, explains why 0.8 exceeds the reconstructed unrounded change. Neither the archive nor the analyst needs to be wrong. Report the operation alongside the number. We have not recovered the unpublished full-precision annual change.

How much can rounding of the published levels alone move July's ratio? If each level is within half a thousand of its displayed integer, positivity of the denominator and monotonicity give the conservative envelope

100(7,163 − 0.5)/(168,429 + 0.5) ≤ r ≤ 100(7,163 + 0.5)/(168,429 − 0.5),
4.252521084% ≤ r ≤ 4.253140056%.

Every number in that interval still rounds to 4.3%. This is a bound under a stated input-rounding assumption, not a sampling confidence interval. Because the numerator and denominator are related, not every corner of that rectangle must be jointly attainable; it nevertheless bounds all values inside. It cannot account for survey error or later revisions.

There is also an accounting residual: June SA has L − E − U = 168,009 − 161,199 − 6,811 = −1 thousand. If underlying values satisfy L* = E* + U* and each displayed value has rounding error of magnitude at most 0.5, the displayed residual is eL − eE − eU, with magnitude at most 1.5 thousand. An integer-valued residual can therefore have magnitude at most 1. This observation makes the −1 compatible with rounding; it does not establish the unknown underlying values. July 2023 NSA similarly has P − L − N = −1 thousand. Keep both residuals visible.

The identity check is deliberately narrow: these two aggregate identities on this six-record extract. Do not generalize it into a demand that every seasonally adjusted subgroup table must add exactly. BLS explains that seasonal adjustment may be performed on component series. A reconciliation rule must follow the actual construction and display precision of the statistic being checked.

Baseline discrepancy log
RecordFindingResolution or limit
D01July ratio 4.252830570%; published 4.3%Nearest-tenth displays agree for all six rates; preserve raw ratios.
D02Annual SA displayed difference 0.8 pp; ratio difference 0.719891780 ppLabel rounding order; neither is an exact full-precision source rate change.
D03Two identities have −1 thousand residualsCompatible with component rounding; retain published integers.
D04Survey estimation and sampling variance are unavailable in this extractNo claim to reconstruct weights, seasonal factors or sampling inference.

Robustness has to answer a declared question

With more time periods or adjustment choices, an analyst can select the comparison that best suits a story. A visible complete grid reduces that discretion. Our grid asks whether the direction of these descriptive changes differs across two adjustment definitions and two horizons. It does not test the same numerical estimand four times: replacing SA with NSA retains recurring seasonal variation; replacing a month with a year changes the comparison interval.

All declared secondary comparisons; pp means percentage points
AdjustmentComparisonRatio difference (pp)Round last (pp)Subtract displayed rates (pp)
SAJuly 2024 − June 20240.1988810790.20.2
SAJuly 2024 − July 20230.7198917800.70.8
NSAJuly 2024 − June 20240.2482617660.20.2
NSAJuly 2024 − July 20230.7430843010.70.7

Every reconstructed change is positive. That limited conclusion survives these four choices. It does not establish a persistent trend from six records, and the two adjustment versions are not independent replications on new respondents. A year comparison also crosses a January population-control update; our extract does not isolate that contribution. A sensitivity check can disclose a changed definition without deciding which definition is appropriate for a new question.

Robustness is a declared check of how conclusions respond to defensible choices. Fishing uses the observed results to choose and present a favorable subset while hiding the search. Exploratory analysis is useful when identified as exploratory. Preserve a specification ledger with the choice, reason, timing and result, including results that weaken the preferred claim. Do not widen a tolerance after seeing a failure and still call the original specification successful. A new tolerance requires a justified new analysis and a retained record of the old one.

What the reconstruction cannot establish

Agreement demonstrates arithmetic and source-definition compatibility for a specified release. Sampling uncertainty remains. The labor-force estimate 168,429 thousand is a population-level estimate, not 168,429,000 independent Bernoulli trials. Putting that number into √[p(1 − p)/n] would invent a sampling design and grossly confuse estimated population size with respondent count. The CPS design, weights, estimation procedures and dependence between monthly estimates matter for uncertainty in a change. This package supplies no survey-standard-error calculation and no significance declaration.

The archived technical note discusses sampling and nonsampling errors, seasonal adjustment and revisions. These limitations are not removed by exact rational arithmetic. Our rounding envelope addresses a much smaller, different issue. It is inappropriate to relabel it “95% confidence,” or to treat an illustrative uncertainty number elsewhere in the note as an estimated interval for this specific result.

The descriptive increase also lacks a treatment definition and counterfactual. Changes in a policy, interest rates or job search may be plausible research topics; this reconstruction identifies none of their causal effects. Nor does it forecast August or establish the performance of a prediction model: there is no fitted forecasting rule, information-time design or held-out evaluation. Use identification and confounding and prediction and validation to formulate those additional tasks.

Run and report the offline reproduction

Download the source extract, analysis data, provenance and hash manifest, standard-library Python benchmark and instructions and rubric into one directory. The preserved benchmark report provides a comparison output. No network call or third-party package is needed:

python3 v04-c12-replication.py
# Or give the directory containing the three required input files:
python3 v04-c12-replication.py /path/to/package

The program validates types, units, keys, release metadata and local file hashes; parses the source extract independently of the analysis JSON; then calculates exact fractions and display values. It reports all six rates, the full comparison grid, component residuals and a discrepancy log. Invalid input produces a diagnostic and a nonzero exit status. A valid but numerically mismatching reconstruction also returns a nonzero status. It never rewrites the frozen inputs. Floating decimals in the output are conveniences; the exact fraction fields preserve the underlying ratio calculations.

A complete report includes: the target and scope; source and access route; observation and release dates; file identifiers and hashes; definitions and units; processing steps and rounding rules; original versus reconstructed results; every declared sensitivity result; discrepancies and unresolved issues; and a bounded conclusion. Record the Python version as execution metadata. An independent reviewer should recompute a few quantities by a different route and inspect the source header, not merely run the same function twice.

Project deliverables: run the package unchanged, preserve its report, independently calculate the baseline and one annual comparison, and submit a one-page replication memo plus a specification ledger. In a separate temporary copy, change June SA labor force to 168,109 thousand, explicitly label it an invented error, and explain why both byte-integrity and identity checks are useful. Preserve the original files. The README supplies scoring criteria and the benchmark numbers; a successful assignment requires both faithful calculation and an honest scope statement.

Exercises

  1. Write the baseline target so another researcher cannot accidentally use a current revised series, an NSA column or a payroll denominator. State the observation month, release date, source-inspection date, population and units. Explain why these dates differ.
  2. Using only the frozen NSA levels, reconstruct July 2024's rate and its change from June. Report the ratio to six decimals, the monthly difference in percentage points to six decimals, their one-decimal displays and the change in unemployed persons. Does the NSA rate reproduce the SA headline?
  3. Reconstruct the SA July-to-July rate change in two ways: difference of published rates and difference of level ratios. Explain their discrepancy numerically using the two display errors. Does either operation recover BLS's undisplayed full-precision estimates?
  4. A memo defines July's unemployment rate as 100U/P, then describes 4.3 − 4.1 as “a 0.2% increase.” Calculate 100U/P and 100U/E from July SA levels, identify the proper denominator, and calculate the relative percent increase implied by the two published rates. Explain why treating the labor-force level as the survey sample size would be another error.
  5. Derive the maximum possible integer residual in L − E − U if an exact underlying identity is preserved and each displayed integer is rounded within half a thousand. Check June SA. In a deliberately corrupted copy, replace its L by 168,109 while keeping E and U fixed. Show that a check of the rounded unemployment rate alone misses this error while the identity check detects it.
  6. Reconstruct the complete four-cell SA/NSA by month/year grid to six decimal places. A researcher presents only the larger NSA monthly change as evidence that a policy caused unemployment. Identify both the reporting problem and the identification problem. State one conclusion supported by the full grid and one it does not support.
  7. An analyst changes whitespace in the JSON without changing any values; another changes a value in both the JSON and text extract and regenerates both hashes. Explain what the benchmark's integrity checks can and cannot establish in these cases. Give a defensible workflow for a newly revised official series.
  8. Write a replication memo of at most 200 words. Include the original targets, reconstructed outputs, release vintage, important discrepancies, scope of success and two remaining inference limits. Describe an independent check and distinguish a rounding envelope from a sampling interval.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. The target is the July 2024 U.S. civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and over household-survey TOTAL, SA unemployment rate and June-to-July changes from Table A-1 and the narrative in the BLS release published 2 August 2024 at 08:30 EDT. Source inspection occurred 7 October 2026. Rates are percent; rate changes are percentage points; levels and their tabular changes are thousands of persons. Use U/L, with L the civilian labor force, not payroll jobs or population. July identifies the observation period, August identifies information availability/vintage, and October 2026 identifies this package's retrieval. Full credit requires all three dates and an explicit SA/household/labor-force specification.
  2. July NSA: 100(7,685/169,723) = 4.527966% to six decimals, displayed 4.5%. June NSA: 100(7,233/169,007) ≈ 4.279704391%. Their difference is 0.248262 percentage point to six decimals, displayed 0.2. The unemployed count rises by 7,685 − 7,233 = 452 thousand = 452,000 persons. These values reconstruct the NSA columns. July's 4.5% does not match the 4.3% SA target because the adjustment definition changed; that is not evidence of an arithmetic failure in the SA reconstruction.
  3. Displayed rates give 4.3 − 3.5 = 0.8 percentage point. Reconstructed ratios give 100(7,163/168,429 − 5,904/167,113) ≈ 0.719891780, displayed 0.7. The display errors are 4.3 − 4.252830570 ≈ +0.047169430 and 3.5 − 3.532938790 ≈ −0.032938790. Subtracting those errors yields +0.080108220; add that to the ratio difference to obtain 0.8. The disagreement is rounding order. Both calculations use already published rounded inputs; neither recovers exact undisplayed estimates.
  4. 100U/P = 100(7,163/268,644) ≈ 2.666354%; 100U/E = 100(7,163/161,266) ≈ 4.441730%. Neither is the unemployment rate, which uses L = E + U conceptually and here gives about 4.252831%. The displayed rate increases by 0.2 percentage point. Its relative increase is 100(4.3/4.1 − 1) ≈ 4.878049%. A relative change formed from the unrounded reconstructed ratios would be another calculation. The estimated number of people in the labor force is not the number of independently sampled respondents; an iid binomial standard error based on it has no justified sampling interpretation here.
  5. Write each displayed count as its underlying count plus e with |e| ≤ 0.5. The exact identity cancels, leaving eL − eE − eU, with magnitude at most 1.5. Because displayed residuals are integers, their magnitude is at most 1. June gives −1 and is compatible. The invented L = 168,109 produces 168,109 − 161,199 − 6,811 = 99 thousand, outside that bound. Yet 100(6,811/168,109) ≈ 4.051538% still rounds to 4.1%. Thus one displayed-rate match misses a serious inconsistency. The untouched manifest also detects the altered file bytes. Do not replace June's actual source value with the invented value.
  6. The grid is SA month 0.198881, SA year 0.719892, NSA month 0.248262 and NSA year 0.743084 percentage point. Their rounding-after-subtraction displays are 0.2, 0.7, 0.2 and 0.7. Subtracting displayed rates instead gives 0.2, 0.8, 0.2 and 0.7. Omitting the other declared specifications selectively reports the larger monthly contrast. Even complete reporting would not identify a policy effect: there is no specified intervention/comparison design establishing the missing counterfactual. Supported: these four descriptive contrasts are positive. Unsupported: a policy caused the change, the increase will persist, or the four cells are independent statistical replications. Alternative unsupported claims receive credit if their missing assumptions are explained.
  7. Whitespace changes the bytes and therefore generally the SHA-256 hash, even when parsed values are unchanged. The unchanged manifest correctly flags departure from the frozen byte artifact. If someone changes both copies and recomputes hashes, local consistency and hashing can pass without truth to the original source; numerical target/identity checks might catch some changes but cannot certify origin. Keep the original package immutable, retrieve the new official vintage into distinctly named files, document its release/retrieval dates and changes, independently inspect the new source, and run a separate analysis. Do not overwrite the old vintage and claim that its reproduction succeeded. Full credit requires both the integrity/provenance distinction and retained original data.
  8. Illustrative memo: “We reconstructed the BLS July 2024 household-survey TOTAL SA unemployment statistics in the 2 August 2024 release. Published targets were 4.3%, a monthly rise of 0.2 percentage point and 352,000 additional unemployed persons. Frozen Table A-1 levels give 100(7,163/168,429) = 4.252830570%, a monthly difference of 0.198881079 percentage point and a 352-thousand count change, matching the target displays. Independent division checked the rate and a separately parsed source extract checked the transcription. Annual SA changes differ by rounding order: displayed rates subtract to 0.8 point; reconstructed ratios differ by 0.719891780 point. Two component identities have −1-thousand residuals compatible with rounding. The success concerns published aggregates, not reconstruction of survey weights or seasonal factors. The July input-rounding envelope, 4.252521084–4.253140056%, is not a sampling interval. No sampling significance, policy effect or forecast has been established.” Evaluate accuracy, units/vintage, evidence for discrepancies, an actual independent calculation, preservation of limits and the 200-word bound; equivalent clear memos are acceptable.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain to a colleague why 0.8 and 0.7 percentage point can both be correctly calculated from one release, why one thousand of nonaddition need not be a bad transcription, and why a matching hash cannot prove official origin. Then state exactly what the replication accomplished in one sentence.

Delayed check, after several days: without the worked examples, reconstruct July's SA rate from U = 7,163 and L = 168,429 thousand; identify the unit of 4.3 − 4.1; describe one failure a rounded-rate check misses; and name one missing ingredient for sampling inference and one for causal inference. Check against 4.252830570% → 4.3%, percentage points, the corrupted-denominator identity example, a justified survey variance calculation and a counterfactual identification design. Revisit the relevant section for each missed distinction.

Next: complete the Volume 4 assessment and integrative project. The later empirical-research work in Volume 12 and Volume 16 extends this bounded reconstruction to econometric designs and research replications. Preserve this chapter's source, target, discrepancy and inference disciplines as the statistical machinery grows.

Sources and further study

  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Employment Situation News Release, July 2024 (2 August 2024 vintage) — Primary empirical source: release date/identifier, Household Survey Data headline targets, full Table A-1 TOTAL column header and selected levels/rates; archived technical-note definitions, reference period, seasonal adjustment, revisions and sampling/nonsampling limits. Supplies six actual historical aggregate records; chapter reconstruction and examples are original.
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Current Population Survey concepts and definitions — Primary definitions of civilian noninstitutional population age16+, United States geography, labor force, unemployed including temporary-layoff search exception, unemployment-rate denominator, participation and seasonal adjustment. Supports interpreting counts as estimated persons rather than survey sample size or payroll jobs.
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Copyright Information — Official public-use basis for the minimal attributed numeric extract, with exceptions for previously copyrighted photographs/illustrations and the separate BLS-emblem limitation. Package reproduces neither images nor emblem.
